lessons.notes: Unit 1 has a prose piece 'The Enchanted Pool' by C. Rajagopalachari (p. 1–22) and a poem 'Upagupta' by Rabindranath Tagore (p. 23–30). The prose is a story from the Mahabharatha: Yudhistira answers the Yaksha's questions and wins back the lives of his brothers. The poem shows the compassion and truthfulness of the Buddhist monk Upagupta towards the dancing girl Vasavadatta. Values: humility, fairness, good conduct, compassion, keeping one's word. Language: prefixes un-/in-/im-; past tense (positive, negative and question forms); Wh-questions; infinitives. Notes on the book: (1) V1 Q2 gives paragraph '(3)' but 'carried away' is in paragraph 2. (2) C3 quotation 5 reads 'Do not follow your brothers', whereas the text reads 'Do not follow them'. (3) The text prints 'Duryodana' (Duryodhana). (4) In the 'Additional Reading' poem the book prints 'Words to Live by' lines without any exercise; it is for discussion.

Check your comprehension – Paragraphs 1 to 3 (p. 3)
1. Who did Yudhistira ask to look for water?
Yudhistira asked Nakula to climb a tree and look for a pool or a river nearby.
2. Why do you think Nakula was happy when he got to the place?
Nakula was happy because he had found a pool of clear water at last, and he could quench his thirst and carry water for his brothers.
3. Can you give a word for 'transparent' which means almost the same?
clear
4. Why do you think Nakula did not obey the voice?
Nakula was so thirsty that he was carried away by his thirst and paid no attention to the warning; so he did not obey the voice.
5. What happened to Nakula when he drank the water?
He felt terribly drowsy at once and fell down, appearing to be dead.
6. Why did Yudhistira send Sahadeva to see what the matter was?
Nakula did not return for a long time, so Yudhistira sent Sahadeva to find out what had happened.
7. Why did Sahadeva meet the same fate as Nakula?
Sahadeva also ignored the warning of the voice and drank the water; so he too dropped down.
Check your comprehension – Paragraphs 4 to 7 (p. 4)
1. What did Arjuna see when he got to the pool?
Arjuna saw his brothers lying near the pool, seeming to be dead.
2. Why do you think the voice did not allow Arjuna to drink water?
The pool belonged to the Yaksha, and he wanted anyone who wished to drink its water to answer his questions first.
3. Why did the invisible being laugh at Arjuna?
Arjuna shot arrows at an unseen being, but the arrows could not touch him; so the Yaksha laughed in scorn at Arjuna's foolish attempt.
4. What was the warning of the Yaksha to Yudhistira?
The Yaksha warned him, 'Your brothers died because they did not heed my words. Do not follow them. Answer my questions first and then quench your thirst. This pool is mine.'
5. Do you observe any difference between Arjuna and Yudhistira in their response to the invisible voice?

Yes. Arjuna became angry, challenged the voice, shot arrows and then drank the water against the warning. Yudhistira remained calm, guessed that it was a Yaksha, obeyed the voice and agreed to answer his questions.
6. Why do you think all the brothers fell unconscious when they drank the water?
The pool belonged to the Yaksha (Yama in disguise) and he had put a spell on its water. Those who drank it without answering his questions fell unconscious.
Check your comprehension – Paragraphs 8 to 15 (p. 7)
1. According to Yudhistira, mind is faster than the wind. Do you agree with him?
Yes, I agree. The mind can reach a faraway place in a moment, but the wind needs time to travel. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.

3. What is the answer of Yudhistira to the question, 'Who rescues man in danger?'

4. Why do you think the Yaksha gave Yudhistira a boon?
The Yaksha was pleased with Yudhistira's wise answers, his patience and his fairness in choosing Nakula, so he gave the boon of life to all his brothers.
5. Why did Yudhistira choose Nakula in preference to Bhima?
Kunti, Yudhistira's mother, would still have one son (Yudhistira) alive, but Madri would be left without any son. To be fair to both mothers, he chose Madri's son Nakula.
6. If you were Yudhistira, how many questions would you be able to answer?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. (ಉದಾ: I would be able to answer some of the questions, such as 'What is faster than wind?')
7. Why did Yama take the form of a Yaksha?
Yama, the lord of Death, took the form of the deer and the Yaksha to see his son Yudhistira and to test him.

C4 – Answer in a short paragraph of 30–40 words (p. 10)
1. 'There must certainly be water there.' How do you think Nakula came to that conclusion?
From the top of the tree, Nakula saw water plants and cranes at a little distance. Water plants grow in water and cranes live near water. So he concluded that there must be a pool or river there.
2. 'Arjuna wanted to destroy this unseen foe.' Why do you think he wanted to do so?
Arjuna was heart-broken to see his three brothers lying dead. He believed that the unseen being had killed them, so he became angry and wanted to avenge their deaths by destroying him.
3. 'Yudhistira himself proceeded in the direction his brothers had taken.' What made Yudhistira take that decision?
Nakula, Sahadeva, Arjuna and Bhima had gone one by one, but none of them returned. Yudhistira became puzzled and worried that something terrible had happened, so he went to find them himself.
4. 'Happiness is the result of good conduct.' Do you agree with this? Support your answer with an example.

Yes, I agree. A person who is honest and kind to others earns love and respect and has peace of mind, which is true happiness. For example, a student who is honest feels free and happy. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
5. 'May the cloud-complexioned Nakula, arise.' Why did Yudhistira choose Nakula in preference to Bhima and Arjuna?
Yudhistira was the son of Kunti, who would still have one living son. Nakula was the son of Madri. To be fair to both mothers, he chose Nakula so that Madri also would not lose all her sons.

Upagupta asleep on the dusty ground of Mathura → The dancing girl invites him to her home → He promises to visit her when the time is ripe → The woman driven away from the town → Upagupta keeps his promise.
Understand the Poem – C3: Quote the lines to justify the qualities (p. 27)
Simplicity
sleeping on the dusty earth – 'Upagupta the disciple of Buddha, lay asleep on the dust by the city wall of Mathura.'
Merciful
'The ascetic sat by her side, took her head on his knees, And moistened her lips with water, and smeared her body with sandal balm'

'the light from a woman's lamp struck his forgiving eyes.'

'She lowered her lamp and saw the young face austerely beautiful.'
Be true to his words
'The time, at last, has come to visit you, and I am here' (he came to her as he had promised)
Understand the Poem – C4: Complete the summary of the poem (p. 27–28)
Upagupta a ______ of Buddha, goes from one place to another.
disciple
Once while he is sleeping in a small town called ______, a dancing girl wakes him up and ______ him to her home.
Mathura; invites
Upagupta ______, but tells her, 'I will visit you when the time is ______'
refuses; ripe
A year later, Upagupta finds the dancing girl lying on the ground ______ the town, having sores all over the body. She is driven away from the ______.
outside; town
He gives her ______ and applies ______ on her body.
water; balm
The woman asks who he is. Upagupta replies, 'Now the ______ has come to visit you and I am here'.
time
Read and Appreciate – R1 (p. 28–29)
1. Why did Upagupta wake up startled?
Upagupta woke up startled because the feet of a woman, tinkling with anklets, suddenly touched his breast and the light of her lamp fell on his eyes.
2. 'The dancing girl was rich.' Do you agree with this opinion? Justify your answer by quoting from the text.
Yes. She was 'starred with jewels', wore 'a pale blue mantle' and was 'drunk with the wine of her youth'. She also had a house to which she invited him.
3. Why do you think the ascetic did not accept the invitation of the dancing girl?
The ascetic was a simple monk who slept on the dusty earth. He felt that the time had not come yet; he promised to come when the time was ripe, that is, when she really needed him.
4. How is the spring season described in the poem?
It was an evening in April. The branches of the wayside trees were full of blossoms and the gay notes of the flute came floating in the warm spring air from afar.
5. 'The time, at last, has come to visit you.' What do you understand by this?
The time when the woman needed help and care most had come. Upagupta had promised to come when the time was ripe; now when she was sick and left alone, he came to serve her.
6. Read the last stanza. Does the description suggest anything about the ascetic?
Yes. It shows that he was merciful, selfless and fearless. He served the woman who was driven away because of her disease, without fear of contagion, and he kept his promise.
Read and Appreciate – R2: Imagery (p. 29)
Identify the images used in the poem and write them down. e.g., 1. Upagupta sleeping on the dusty ground.

1. Upagupta sleeping on the dusty ground.
2. Lamps out, doors shut, stars hidden by the murky sky of August.
3. The tinkling anklets of the dancing girl touching his breast.
4. The dancing girl starred with jewels, wearing a pale blue mantle.
5. The black night showing its teeth in a flash of lightning; the storm growling from the corner of the sky.
6. The wayside trees full of blossoms in April; flute notes floating in the warm air.
7. The woman lying in the shadow of the mango grove, her body spotted with sores.
8. The ascetic taking her head on his knees, moistening her lips with water and smearing sandal balm.
Read and Appreciate – R3 and Do the project (p. 29)
R3. In groups of four discuss what might have happened next in the story of the poem 'Upagupta'. Share your answer with the rest of the class.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. ಸೂಚಿತ ಮಾದರಿ: The woman recovered with Upagupta's care. She understood his kindness, gave up her proud life and became his follower.
Do the project – Think of the incident critically. Think of irony in the books you have studied. Share your opinions with your classmates.

Irony – when the dancing girl invited the ascetic, he refused; but when she was sick and left alone, he came and served her, and she could not even recognise him. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
Recite and enjoy – 'Words to Live by' (p. 30)
Read the poem 'Words to Live by'. Do you find any similarity between the poem 'Upagupta' and this one? Discuss.

Yes. Both poems value kindness and giving to others over wealth and fame. The poem says that it is not how much we accomplish but how much we give to others that counts; Upagupta did the same by serving the sick woman. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.

lessons.words: messenger – a person carrying a message; council – group of people chosen to advise; hermit – a person who lives alone and leads a simple life; affairs – things/matters/business; beds – small patches of ground for plants; spade – tool for digging; fainted – lost consciousness; seized – took by force; faithful – loyal and true; fatally – seriously; sobbing – crying; comfort – to make somebody, who is worried, feel better; aid – help; arduous – involving a lot of effort or energy
lessons.notes: Unit 2 has a prose piece 'The Three Questions' by Count Leo Tolstoy (p. 31–42) and a poem 'Gratefulness' by Joseph T. Renaldi (p. 43–45), which is for memorization. The king finds that the most important time is 'Now', the most important person is the one we are with, and the most important business is to do that person good. The poem teaches gratitude for eyes, ears, lips, mind, hands, prayer and, above all, a loving heart. Language: forms of words (noun/verb), phrases, active and passive voice, compound sentences with coordinating conjunctions (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so – 'FANBOYS'). Notes on the book: (1) 'Language in Use – L2' (compound sentences) has explanation and examples only; there is no written task. (2) The Self-assessment table is for the child's own ticking.
ab: Before You Read – Discuss in groups (p. 31)
Discuss: The best time to do something. / The most important person in your life. / The most important thing to do in your life.
ಸೂಚಿತ ಮಾದರಿ: The best time to do something is 'now'. The most important person in my life is my mother. The most important thing to do in life is to help others. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
Check Your Comprehension – Paragraphs 1 to 3 (p. 33)
1. What thought came to the king?
The king thought that he would never fail if he knew three things: the right time to begin something, whom he should listen to, and the most important thing to do.
2. Write the three questions for which the king wanted to have answers.

1. What is the right time to begin something?
2. Who should a king listen to?
3. What is the most important thing for a king to do?
3. Was the king satisfied with the answers? If 'yes', why? If 'no', why?
No. The wise men answered the questions in different ways, so the king was not satisfied.
4. Who did the king decide to seek advice from?
He decided to seek the advice of a hermit who was widely known for his wisdom.
Check your comprehension – Paragraphs 4 to 7 (p. 34)
1. How did the king treat the wounded person?
The king washed the wound, covered it with his handkerchief and re-dressed it until the bleeding stopped. He also stayed with him through the night.
2. Why did the bearded man swear revenge on the king?
The king had put the man's brother to death and seized his property, so the man swore revenge on him.
3. Who had wounded the man and why?
The king's bodyguard wounded him because he recognised him as the king's enemy when he came out of his hiding place.
4. Why did the man say that he would serve the king as his most faithful servant?
The man wanted to kill the king, but the king saved his life by dressing his wounds. Out of gratitude he decided to serve the king faithfully.
Check Your Comprehension – Paragraphs 8 to 10 (p. 35)
1. What did the king promise the man?
The king promised to forgive him and give back his property.
2. The hermit said that the king had been answered. If you agree, what was the answer to the first question?
Yes, I agree. The right time to do something is 'now', the present moment (when the king was digging the beds and when he was caring for the wounded man).
3. Why did the hermit say that he was the most important man?

When the king was digging the beds for the hermit, the hermit was the person with him. Had the king not helped him, he would have gone away and the enemy would have attacked him. So at that time the hermit was the most important man.
4. According to the hermit, 'now' is the most important time. Why?
Because 'now' is the only time we have any power to act.
5. What according to the hermit, was the most important business?
To do good to the person we are with at a particular moment, because we are sent into this world for that purpose alone.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. ಉದಾಹರಣೆ: 'Three terrorists were shot dead.' – passive; 'Police arrest two thieves.' – active; 'Rain floods the city.' – active; 'A new bridge was opened yesterday.' – passive.
Speak well – Offering help (p. 40–41)
Work in pairs playing the role of Abdul and James and practise the conversation at Golgumbaz.
ಮೌಖಿಕ ಅಭ್ಯಾಸ – ಲಿಖಿತ ಉತ್ತರ ಅಗತ್ಯವಿಲ್ಲ (ಶಿಕ್ಷಕರ ಸೂಚನೆ).
Practise writing – Story using the clues (p. 41–42)

Discuss in groups and write a story using the clues: A small lonely railway station of a remote village … bad winter night … dogs howling … no lights … A passenger waiting for the train … train arrives … gets into the compartment … only one traveller is there … he asks the new incumbent if he believed in ghosts … this man says 'no' … the other traveller disappears.

ಸೂಚಿತ ಮಾದರಿ – A Night at the Station: It was a bad winter night at a small, lonely railway station in a remote village. Dogs were howling and there were no lights. A passenger was waiting for the train. At last the train arrived and he got into a compartment. Only one traveller was sitting there. After some time the traveller asked him, 'Do you believe in ghosts?' The passenger said, 'No.' Then the traveller smiled and said, 'But I am one!' and disappeared. The passenger was shocked and sat trembling till the next station. (Moral/Title: The Ghost in the Compartment) ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
Present the story to the class. Try to narrate it using voice modulation, facial expressions etc.
ಮೌಖಿಕ ಅಭ್ಯಾಸ – ಲಿಖಿತ ಉತ್ತರ ಅಗತ್ಯವಿಲ್ಲ (ಶಿಕ್ಷಕರ ಸೂಚನೆ).
Self-assessment (p. 42)
Read the statements and put a tick mark in the appropriate box.
ವಿದ್ಯಾರ್ಥಿಯ ಸ್ವಯಂ ಮೌಲ್ಯಮಾಪನ – ಮಗು ತನಗೆ ಅನ್ವಯಿಸುವ ಪೆಟ್ಟಿಗೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಟಿಕ್ (✓) ಮಾಡಬೇಕು. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
POETRY – Gratefulness: Before you read (p. 43)
1. Was Sunita right in being angry with God?
No. Her anger was not right because she was alive and could recover, while many people suffer from birth.
2. How did Anjali comfort Sunita?
Anjali told her to look at those who are physically challenged since birth and to be grateful to the creator.
3. Who should we be grateful to? Why?
We should be grateful to God (the creator), because he has given us our eyes, ears, lips, hands, a mind and a heart. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
Understand the poem (p. 45)
1. Why is the poet grateful for eyes and ears?
The poet is grateful for eyes because he can see the activities that he can do, and for ears because he can hear the sobbing of those who need him near.
2. How do lips and mind help a human being?
The lips help us to speak words of comfort and peace to all who seek them, and the mind helps us to know how to aid those who need us.
3. What does the poet use his hands for?
The poet uses his hands to do some arduous (difficult) or simple task for others.
4. Why does the poet place the heart above all else?
Because the heart was given to him so that he may love; love is the greatest gift and it makes all other gifts useful.
Read and appreciate (p. 45)
1. Pick out the rhyming words from the poem. (see–me, speak–seek)
see – me; hear – near; speak – seek; know – so; do – you; pray – day; above – love
2. Which stanza do you like the most? Why?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. ಸೂಚಿತ ಮಾದರಿ: I like the last stanza the most because it says that a heart to love is the greatest gift.
3. Try and translate the poem into your mother tongue.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.

lessons.t: Unit 3 · My Beginnings (Prose) & A Girl Called Golden (Poem)
lessons.words: nestle – to be surrounded by something, especially hills or countryside; regale – to entertain someone by telling them about something; naughty – behaving badly; castles in the air – plans or hopes that are unlikely ever to become real; ambition – a strong desire to achieve something; bunk – to leave a place (school) without telling anyone; amuse – to make someone laugh or smile; perched on – to be in a position on top of something or at the edge of something; walloping – hitting someone very hard; clumsy – done carelessly or badly; scrambling on – to move somewhere in a hurried awkward way; fright – a sudden feeling of fear; tether – to tie an animal with a rope or chain so that it cannot move far; anticipate – to expect that something will happen and be ready for it; venture – to do or try something that involves risks; imperceptibly – almost impossible to see or notice; studious – spending a lot of time studying and reading; fence – a barrier put around a field or an area; claim – to state that something is true, even though it has not been proved; offer – to say that you are willing to do something; saddle – a leather seat that you sit on when you ride a horse; sprint – to run or go very fast for a short distance; coach – a person who teaches and trains an athlete or performer; spurred – (here) encouraged to try harder to achieve something; spells – (here) a period of time; heed – to pay careful attention to somebody's advice or warning; glory – fame, praise or honour
lessons.notes: Unit 3 has a prose piece 'My Beginnings' by Kapil Dev (p. 46–65), an extract from his autobiography 'Straight from the Heart', and a poem 'A Girl Called Golden' by David Bateson (p. 66–70), an ode to the Australian sprinter Betty Cuthbert. Values: determination, hard work, love of sports, kindness in sport. Language: primary auxiliaries (be, do, have) in present and past, positive and negative; subject–verb agreement; the word 'sport/sports'. Notes on the book: (1) The glossary meaning of 'tether' (to be so tired…) and 'fence' (a structure that horses jump over) does not suit the text; the correct meanings used here are 'to tie an animal with a rope' and 'a barrier put around an area'. (2) Check-your-comprehension Q1 (p. 50) says '7th paragraph' but the naughty act (riding police horses) is in the 5th paragraph. (3) The table in 'Practise writing' prints 'Mardona' (Maradona). (4) The recite-and-enjoy poem 'Missed' by P.G. Wodehouse has no exercise. (5) The V3 cricket-field figure has 23 empty boxes; the positions are given below as a list (teacher to verify against the figure).
ab: Before You Read – Gandhiji's extract (p. 46)
Was Gandhiji right in his opinion? If yes, why? If not, why?

At that time Gandhiji's opinion that gymnastics had nothing to do with education was wrong, and he himself later said so. Physical training should have as much place in the curriculum as mental training. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
'Should sports and games be made compulsory in schools and colleges?' Discuss.
ಸೂಚಿತ ಮಾದರಿ: Yes. Sports keep us healthy, teach teamwork and discipline and make the mind alert. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
Check your comprehension – Paragraphs 1 and 2 (p. 47)
1. Kapil says, 'The date, 6th January 1959, was thankfully recorded.' Why does he feel so?
His mother could not read the time and nobody noted his birth date. But a cousin of his was born on the same day with the same name, so the date was recorded and Kapil came to know it.
2. Kapil says, 'But at that time…these dreams seemed like castles in the air.' What were these dreams? Were these dreams realized?
His dreams were to travel around the world and to drive a Mercedes Benz. Yes, both dreams were fulfilled.
3. What did Kapil's mother always regale him with?
She always regaled him with tales of his naughty behaviour.
4. Kapil uses an idiomatic expression 'castles in the air'. What does this mean?
'Castles in the air' means plans or hopes that are unlikely ever to become real.
Check your comprehension – Paragraphs 3 and 4 (p. 48–49)
1. In what way was Kapil 'like all the other children' around him?
Like other children, he tried to bunk school, saved money to see a new movie or eat chicken chowmein with friends, and when bored, plucked fruit from the neighbour's tree.
2. In the third paragraph Kapil says that the lady in the neighbourhood grew trees. What were the two trees grown there?
The two trees were papaya and pomegranate.
3. How did Kapil and his friends spend most of their time in their childhood?
They spent most of their time planning how to get into the lady's garden and pick the fruit off the trees.
4. What had Kapil done that he had to sit still for two hours?
Kapil and his friend had climbed over the wall and were perched on the papaya tree when the lady came out with her guests for tea right under it. So they had to sit still till the tea party ended.
5. What discovery did Kapil make by sitting on the papaya tree?
He discovered the rash that papaya sap can cause.
6. 'She counted them every day.' What did the lady count every day? Why? 'I got even the next day.' What does this mean? What does this tell us about Kapil?

The lady counted the ninety-two pomegranates on her tree every day because she knew the children were up to mischief. 'I got even' means 'I took revenge'; the next day, when she went to Delhi, Kapil and his friends took down all the pomegranates. It shows that Kapil was naughty, daring and full of mischief.
Check your comprehension – Paragraphs 5 to 7 (p. 49–50)
1. What naughty thing does Kapil narrate in the 7th paragraph? (Note: the naughty thing is narrated in the 5th paragraph.)
Kapil narrates how he and his friends rode the police horses that were left to graze in the open green areas, and how he tried to take one horse home.
2. 'Nobody would have noticed except for the fact that I bit off more than I could chew.' What is the incident described here?

Kapil took a police horse out of the fenced area and tried to house it in the small back garden of his house, but he could not get the animal through the tiny doorway and they were caught within minutes.
3. Why does Kapil say he bit off more than he could chew?
He tried to do something that was too difficult for him – taking a huge horse through a tiny doorway of five and a half feet by two feet.
4. How did Kapil's father react to his escapade?
His father scolded him (chided him); the scolding discouraged Kapil from going near the grazing fields again.
5. What were the games offered in the local school where Kapil was studying?
Basketball, football, table tennis and hockey.
6. Which game was Kapil fairly good at during his school days?
Kapil was fairly good at all games and exceptionally good at athletics; he dreamed of becoming a footballer and played football for his school.
7. 'That is a decision I will always be grateful to them for, as they unconsciously introduced me to the game for which I was made.' What was the 'decision'?
The decision was to change his game from football to cricket, as his friends convinced him.
8. 'But it was all merely fun to start with.' What is Kapil talking about? Do you think cricket remained merely fun for him forever?

He is talking about playing cricket in the beginning. No, cricket did not remain merely fun; it became his profession and he became India's greatest all-rounder and captain of the 1983 World Cup winning team.
C1 – Arrange the sentences in the right order (p. 52)
Arrange sentences a to h in the right order.

a → f → d → b → c → g → h → e
(a. A lady lived down the road and she had a beautiful garden. → f. She took great pride in the papaya and pomegranate trees. → d. One day Kapil and his friends climbed over the wall and perched on the tree. → b. She entertained the guests for tea right under the papaya tree. → c. Two others were on the road, on the other side of the wall. → g. Two friends who had been outside ran away. → h. But Kapil and his friend had to sit for nearly two hours. → e. That was the day Kapil discovered the rash that papaya sap can cause.)
C2 – True or False (p. 52–53)
a. Kapil was born into a large family.
True (he had six other brothers and sisters).
b. Kapil came to know about the date of his birth from his mother.
False (his mother could not read the time; the date was recorded because a cousin was born on the same day).
c. The lady who was a neighbour to Kapil counted ninety-two pomegranates on the tree in her garden because she was good at mathematics.
False (she counted them because she knew the children were up to mischief).
d. The police horses became Kapil's pet.
False (they were police horses; he rode them and the horse was returned).
e. Kapil was good at athletics and dreamed of becoming a footballer.
True
C3 – Narrate Kapil's childhood experiences to your friend (p. 53)
Begin: Kapil shares two very interesting incidents with the reader.

Kapil shares two very interesting incidents with the reader. In the first, Kapil and his friends climbed a neighbour's wall and sat on her papaya tree to steal fruit. Suddenly the lady came with her guests for tea right under the tree, so Kapil and his friend had to sit still for two hours. He also got a rash from papaya sap. The next day he took away all ninety-two pomegranates from her tree. In the second incident, Kapil rode the police horses left to graze and tried to keep one in his back garden, but could not take it through the small doorway and was caught. His father scolded him and he never went near the horses again. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.

athletics (because the other three are all 'ball games')
2. coach, learner, teacher, trainer
learner (because the others are persons who teach or train)
3. boxing, running, jumping, throwing
boxing (because the others are athletic events/track and field events)
4. stamina, speed, skill, sports
sports (because the others are qualities/abilities of a sportsperson)
5. victory, success, defeat, win
defeat (because the others mean winning)
6. medal, shield, cup, competition

'Them' stands for our actions and words – whatever we do or say.
2. Imagine that a parent of your friend says, 'Work only for the result'. How would you respond to this statement?

I would say politely that the result is important, but how we work, our effort and the way we do it are also important, and we should try to do everything better and better. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.

Words with action and action with words make a situation more pleasant. For example, the two men removing the packets could have said, 'One minute sir, we'll finish in no time', and the author could have lent a helping hand to them.
6. What sort of word and what kind of action would make any situation better?
Polite, kind and pleasant words such as 'Yes sir?', 'Please' and 'Thank you', and helpful actions such as a smile, a gesture or a helping hand, would make any situation better.

Doctors can improve their image by talking nicely and reassuringly to the patients; a couple of friendly words or a smile can make the patient feel better.

The first auto driver did not look at the author and just 'downed' the meter without any word or gesture. The second driver said 'No' pleasantly: he said he had to hand over the auto and helped the author by asking another driver, 'Guru, Central market?'

We should give it gracefully, with kind words and some feeling, such as 'Here, take this', and not grudgingly or with a rude gesture.

According to the author, public notices should be made more polite and polished, like 'Thank You for Not Smoking' or 'Please make room for waiting customers', and not rough like 'No Parking' or 'Don't sit here for a long time'.

Language in use – Simple Present Tense: II Activity 'Something special' (p. 84–85)
Write one interesting present fact about yourself and read your friend's facts using he/she.

2. You have to attend an important family function tomorrow. Therefore, you will not be able to attend classes. Write a note informing your friend/classmate about this and asking him/her to help you with the lessons/class notes.

I have to attend an important family function tomorrow, so I will not be able to come to school. Please note down the lessons and the homework for me. I will collect your notes the day after tomorrow. Thank you.

(Date) ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
POETRY – The Wonderful Words: Before you read (p. 87)
1. Look at the words and phrases in the box and mime them: astonished, thanking someone, requesting for help, being happy, feel nervous, apologizing to someone, helping a blind person cross the road.
ಮೌಖಿಕ ಅಭ್ಯಾಸ – ಲಿಖಿತ ಉತ್ತರ ಅಗತ್ಯವಿಲ್ಲ (ಶಿಕ್ಷಕರ ಸೂಚನೆ).
2. Suppose you have been to a strange place where people use a language which is different from yours / new to you. How will you communicate with them in that situation? Discuss with your friends.
I will communicate using gestures, body language, facial expressions, pictures, simple words and by asking someone who knows both languages to help. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
Understand the poem – I (p. 88)
1. What does the poet ask us not to let die?
The poet asks us not to let a thought shrivel and die for want of a way to say it.
2. 'English is a game to play.' How does the poet justify it?
The poet says that all we have to do is to match the words to the brightest thoughts in our head so that they come out clear and true; so anyone can play this game of English.
3. The poet speaks about matching words. What should we match the words with?
We should match the words with the brightest thoughts in our head.
4. What has never been said yet, according to the poet?
Many of the loveliest things have never yet been said.
5. 'Words are the food and dress of thought / They give it its body and swing.' What do you understand by these lines?
Just as food gives energy and dress gives shape and beauty to the body, words give life, form and rhythm to a thought. Without words, thoughts cannot be expressed.
6. What does everyone try to hear and see afresh?
Everyone is longing to hear some fresh and beautiful thing.
7. The poet mentions 'prison' in line 16. What according to her, is imprisoned?
A thought is imprisoned behind our eyes (in our mind); only words can set it free.
Read and appreciate – II (p. 88–89)
1. Which lines in the poem strike you the most? Can you think of some other lines which are highly thought-provoking? Discuss in a small group and share your responses.
ಉದಾಹರಣೆ: 'But only words can free a thought from its prison behind your eyes'; 'For many of the loveliest things have never yet been said'. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
2. 'Words alone are good' says a great Indian poet. Can you relate the meaning of the statement with the theme of the poem you have studied?
Yes. Both say that words are valuable, because only through good words can our thoughts reach others. In the poem, words give a body to thought. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
3. Our philosophy advocates the oneness-unanimity of Kaya (work), Vaacha (speech) and Manasa (thoughts). How far does this poem support this philosophy?

The poem supports it to a great extent. It says that our thoughts (manasa) should be expressed clearly and truly through words (vaacha), and good thoughts and words lead to good actions (kaya). ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.

lessons.t: Supplementary Reading · Aruna Asaf Ali – The Great Patriot and The Happy Cure
lessons.au: Edited (Aruna Asaf Ali); Retold by Rose Dobbs (The Happy Cure)
lessons.words: fiery – having a great deal of energy; raging – filled with anger; convention – doing things the way most people consider to be right; prosecuted – officially charged with a crime in court; callous – very cruel, incapable of tender emotions; concede – to give in, yield; solitary confinement – a punishment in which a prisoner is kept alone in a separate cell; got wind of – got the clue of an idea; warrant – an official order signed by a magistrate which empowers the police to arrest a person or search his house; cordon – a protective barricade created by police personnel or vehicles to prevent people from entering the area; stand in for – to act on behalf of someone; impulse – a sudden inexplicable urge to do something; helter-skelter – in disorderly haste or confusion; defy – openly resist or refuse to obey; going underground – hiding from the law to avoid detection; posthumous – an award or honour given to a person after his/her death; groan – make a sad sound when in pain; moan – a painful sound; sharp stabs – pricking; physician – doctor; surgeons – doctors who perform surgeries (operations); dolts – stupid persons; courtiers – persons who are part of the court of a king; peer – look closely; instantly – immediately; summon – call for a meeting; politely – in a gentle manner; trembled – shook slightly; resolve – decide; fancied – imagined
lessons.notes: The Supplementary Reading has two pieces: 'Aruna Asaf Ali – The Great Patriot' (p. 90–94), a biography of the freedom fighter who hoisted the national flag at Gowalia Tank Maidan on 9 August 1942, and 'The Happy Cure' (p. 95–98), a story by Rose Dobbs about a bored king who imagines he is ill. Exercises: Aruna Asaf Ali – I. two or three sentences; II. four or five sentences. The Happy Cure – ten questions in two or three sentences each. Values: patriotism and courage; contentment, and the need to be busy doing good. Note on the book: the text prints 'stroke their beards' (stroked) and the Q4 of Aruna Asaf Ali says 'Gandhi's arrest' while the text says the top leaders including Gandhiji were arrested.
ab: Aruna Asaf Ali – I. Answer in two or three sentences each (p. 94)
1. What kind of atmosphere existed in the country when Aruna entered politics?
The freedom struggle was raging in the country and the youth were laying down their lives for the country's independence when Aruna plunged headlong into politics.
2. Why was she termed a non-conformist?

She was born into an orthodox Hindu Bengali family, but she broke conventions at the age of 19 by marrying Asaf Ali, a prominent figure in the freedom struggle who was twenty years older than her. So she was called a non-conformist.
3. What was the impact of Aruna's public address during the Salt Satyagraha?

Her public meetings and processions during the Salt Satyagraha made her a political leader; she was prosecuted and sentenced to one year imprisonment, and when she was not released, a public agitation was launched in her support.
4. Why had the Committee planned to hoist the tricolour? What had led to Gandhi's arrest before the hoisting of the flag?

The Quit India resolution was passed on 8 August 1942 at the Bombay Congress Session, and the Committee planned to hoist the tricolour at Gowalia Tank Maidan. The British got wind of the plan and arrested the top leaders including Gandhiji a few hours before the event.
5. 'There's no arrest warrant for you, Madam.' Whom else was the warrant given to? What did Aruna persuade the British sergeant to do?
The warrant was given to her husband, Asaf Ali. Aruna persuaded the British sergeant to let her accompany them to the railway station to see off her husband.
Aruna Asaf Ali – II. Answer in four–five sentences each (p. 94)
1. Describe the scene at Victoria Terminus in the early hours of August 9, 1942, as witnessed by Aruna Asaf Ali.

Dawn was about to break. There was a cordon around Victoria Terminus to keep the crowds at bay. A special train was standing at the platform. As Aruna walked along the platform she saw Maulana Azad sitting at a window in a compartment, and she stopped to talk to him. He was to unfurl the tricolour at Gowalia Tank Maidan at 8 a.m. and she made up her mind to go there.
2. Narrate an instance from the biography to justify the fact that the British were extremely autocratic and ruthless.

At Gowalia Tank Maidan, the meeting was declared illegal under Section 144 and a sergeant gave the crowd only two minutes to disperse. Hardly had the flag been unfurled when the police lobbed tear gas shells into the crowd. The men and women ran helter-skelter with tears streaming down their cheeks. Also, the leaders were arrested early in the morning without any warning.
3. Why was Aruna Asaf Ali considered the Grand Old Lady of the freedom struggle?

She plunged into politics when the freedom struggle was raging. She led processions in the Salt Satyagraha, went to jail, went on a hunger strike against the callous treatment of prisoners, hoisted the national flag in 1942, which marked the start of the Quit India Movement, and worked underground as the editor of 'Inquilaab'. Hence she was called the 'Grand Old Lady of the Independence movement'.
4. What was Aruna's advice to the freedom fighters?

She advised the freedom fighters not to allow any academic arguments on questions like violence and non-violence to divert attention from the stern realities of the day. She wanted every student and youth to think and feel as soldiers of the nation that is to come.
5. What was Gandhiji's advice to Aruna? Why could she not abide by it?

Gandhiji advised her to come out of hiding and surrender because she had become ill and was reduced to a skeleton, and to take the reward money for the great Indian cause. She did not follow it because she was determined to continue the movement underground; she surrendered only when the warrants for her arrest were cancelled on 26 January 1946.
6. What were the awards given to Aruna? Why were they given?

She was awarded the Nehru Award for International Understanding in 1992 and the Bharat Ratna, the highest civilian honour, posthumously. They were given for her great service in the freedom struggle and for her social work, especially for women, after independence.
The Happy Cure – Answer in two or three sentences each (p. 98)
1. 'The king was foolish.' Do you agree with this statement? Justify your answer quoting one incident from the text.

Yes, I agree. The king was not ill but only bored, yet he insisted that he was dying. When the doctors found nothing wrong, he called them dolts and idiots and threatened that the next one who found nothing wrong would have his ears cut off and nose shortened. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
2. 'Physicians and surgeons are dolts.' Why did the king call them dolts?
The physicians and surgeons examined him but could find nothing wrong with him, whereas the king believed that he was a very sick man; so he called them dolts (stupid persons).
3. What did the simple woman say to the king after she peered into his face?
She said, 'Your majesty, you are suffering from a strange and rare disease. So rare and strange that no name exists for it.'
4. 'You will be cured instantly,' said the simple old woman. What was the cure suggested?
She suggested that the king should sleep for one night in the shirt of a happy man.
5. Why did the soldiers and courtiers, messengers and heralds have to travel far and wide?
They had to find a happy man and bring his shirt to the king; so they travelled from east to west and north to south across the kingdom.
6. 'I sing from joy,' said the stranger. Why do you think the stranger sang from joy?
The stranger was happy because he loved his fellow men, owned but little and wanted less. He was content with what he had.
7. Why did the king hang his head in shame? What did he resolve afterwards?

The king was ashamed because the cure had been right there all the time: the happy man did not even own a shirt, and only his own folly had made him think he was ill. He resolved to be a good king, to help his people and to rule wisely and well.
8. Do you think the title of the story is appropriate? Give reasons.
Yes. The king was cured by learning from a happy man that contentment and being busy in doing good are the real cure. So 'The Happy Cure' is appropriate. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
9. 'People who have nothing to do are bored to death.' Explain this statement.
People who have no work or interest feel so bored and unhappy that life seems tiresome, almost like a disease. The king in the story was not ill, he was suffering from having nothing to do.
10. Suggest another title to the story.
The Shirt of a Happy Man / The Bored King / The King's Folly. (Any suitable title)
